record.paper_title: Open questions in massive star research
record.original_question: What fraction of observed Wolf-Rayet stars were stripped of their hydrogen-rich envelopes by a binary companion rather than produced by single-star mass loss and mixing? This includes the unresolved subproblem of how many Wolf-Rayet stars were stripped only after the initially more massive star had already become a compact object, a channel whose rate depends on uncertain compact-object natal kicks and common-envelope evolution.

evidence.quote: 4.3. Which fraction of the Wolf-Rayet stars were stripped by a companion?
The fraction of Wolf-Rayet stars produced in this way is uncertain, mostly due to uncertainties in the formation kicks of compact objects, and in the common envelope physics.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
A Wolf–Rayet (WR) star is a hot, hydrogen-depleted massive star showing broad emission lines from a strong stellar wind. Two principal evolutionary channels produce WR stars:

(i) Single-star evolution, in which an initially massive star sheds its hydrogen-rich envelope through stellar winds and rotational/convective mixing without the influence of a companion.

(ii) Binary stripping, in which the hydrogen-rich envelope is removed by mass transfer to (or common-envelope evolution with) a binary companion. Within channel (ii) there is a distinguished sub-channel in which the companion is already a compact object (neutron star or black hole) at the time of stripping; the prevalence of this sub-channel depends on the natal kicks imparted to compact objects at formation and on the physics of common-envelope evolution.

Let N_obs denote the total population of observed WR stars (in a chosen galaxy or galactic environment, e.g., the Milky Way, the Large Magellanic Cloud, or the Small Magellanic Cloud).

Problem. Determine, as a function of metallicity and host environment:

(a) the fraction f_bin = N_bin / N_obs of observed WR stars whose hydrogen-rich envelope was removed primarily by interaction with a binary companion, as opposed to being produced by single-star mass loss and mixing;

(b) the sub-fraction f_co ≤ f_bin of observed WR stars that were stripped only after the initially more massive component had already collapsed into a compact object, quantifying the dependence of f_co on the assumed distributions of compact-object natal kicks and on the prescriptions for common-envelope evolution.
artifact.status_search_result: Estimates vary widely and remain unsettled. Synthetic population models predict that up to ~80% of WR stars in the LMC may be products of binary interaction, yet only ~40% are observed as binaries; in the SMC, models predict ≳98% binary WR fraction but observations show far fewer. The compact-object-stripping sub-channel remains highly uncertain due to poorly constrained natal kicks and common-envelope physics. The question is actively studied (e.g., LMC synthetic populations, 2022; WR–compact object binary progenitor studies, 2024–2025) and is not considered solved.

status_evidence.title: A synthetic population of Wolf-Rayet stars in the LMC
status_evidence.snippet: Synthetic WR population predicts ~80% of WR stars in binary systems while only ~40% of LMC WR stars are known binaries.
status_evidence.claim: Binary-stripped fraction predicted by models substantially exceeds the observed binary fraction; the true fraction is still debated.

status_evidence.title: Why binary interaction does not necessarily dominate the formation of Wolf-Rayet stars at low metallicity
status_evidence.snippet: Binary stripping fraction depends non-trivially on metallicity and WR definitions; binary channel does not necessarily dominate.
status_evidence.claim: The dominance of binary stripping in producing WR stars is unresolved and metallicity-dependent.

status_evidence.title: Wolf-Rayet–compact object binaries as progenitors of binary compact objects
status_evidence.snippet: Recent population synthesis study (2024) of WR+compact-object systems; rates depend strongly on natal kicks and common-envelope prescriptions.
status_evidence.claim: The sub-channel involving stripping after the companion is already a compact object remains uncertain due to natal-kick and common-envelope physics.
